Louis later discovers she had marked six traps in the bylaws.
plays.why_it_works: Beating the toughest person in the building establishes a reputation faster than any number of quiet wins. Using the opponent's own rules makes the attack hard to reverse, because objecting means rejecting his own work.
plays.outcome: She wins the fight, but Louis calls in a favor with Harvey, who orders her to give the case back. The win damages her relationship with Harvey and shows her that her position depends on him.
plays.counter: Louis could have accepted the loss gracefully, as Jessica Pearson advised; that would have denied Scottie the fight she wanted and made him an ally.
plays.principle: To establish yourself fast, beat the strongest person in the room with their own rules, and pick a win your sponsor will not have to overturn.
plays.in_practice: A newcomer needs an early visible win, but choose one that does not force your sponsor to take sides, or it can be reversed over your head.

quote.text: I win this, I'm the partner that beat Louis Litt, not the partner sleeping with Harvey Specter.
quote.speaker: Dana Scott

plays.title: Timing the Empty Chair
plays.target: Harvey Specter (and Jessica Pearson's authority)
plays.context: Jack Soloff, an ambitious partner, has just become head of the compensation committee and wants to make his name. Harvey Specter earns heavily from contingency fees, and his protector is Jessica Pearson, the managing partner.
plays.play: Jack drafts a 'neutral' change in the pay formula toward billable hours that hits Harvey hardest, and frames it as fairness for the firm's grinders against its rainmakers. He pitches it to Louis Litt first, and schedules it for a partners' meeting Jessica will miss. Louis lets it come to the floor, planning to knock it down and prove his loyalty to Harvey, but Harvey rebuffs Louis's help and storms out. Jack counts his votes, 45%, and waits for the rest.
plays.why_it_works: A general rule that happens to hurt one person is harder to oppose than a direct attack, and 'grinders versus rainmakers' builds a coalition of the many against the few. Choosing a meeting without the protector removes the one person able to kill the proposal.
plays.outcome: The vote passes and Harvey's pay is cut, helped along when Louis, caught short, leaks Harvey's income statements. Louis's plan to invite the attack so he could defend Harvey fails, because Harvey reads the defense as condescension.
plays.counter: Jessica could have required major policy changes to wait for a full meeting, and Harvey could have accepted Louis's public support in place of alienating his only ally in the room.
plays.principle: Attack a person through a principle many people benefit from, and pick the moment their protector is away.
plays.in_practice: Proposals framed as fairness for the majority gain momentum fast. If you are the outlier, engage early, bring allies, and never let governance changes land in a meeting you cannot attend.

quote.text: On top of that, Jessica's not gonna be at the meeting tomorrow. Timing couldn't be better.
quote.speaker: Jack Soloff

plays.title: The Snap Vote
plays.target: Louis Litt
plays.context: Jessica Pearson has left the firm, and Harvey Specter has been avoiding telling Louis Litt that he is taking over as managing partner. Louis is refusing to give up control of the associates or to accept Donna Paulsen as a partner, and Donna demands a vote on her status.
plays.play: Harvey confronts Louis in front of Donna and defends her partnership. Then he says that he, and nobody else, decides when votes happen, and calls one on the spot, declaring himself managing partner. He warns that if it is not unanimous there will be a big problem, and asks Louis directly whether he has a problem with Harvey calling the shots.
plays.why_it_works: Calling the vote in a heated moment, with a new ally in the room and no time for Louis to organize, makes dissent costly and isolated. Asking the question personally forces a public commitment Harvey can hold Louis to later.
plays.outcome: Louis says yes, and in the next episode Harvey reminds him of that answer when Louis objects to a new hire.
plays.counter: Louis could have asked for time to consider, or negotiated terms such as his own title, before agreeing.
plays.principle: Settle who is in charge while your support is in the room and your rival is off balance, then hold them to their answer.
plays.in_practice: When a leadership change is needed, make it explicit and get clear agreement from the key people at once, before ambiguity sets in, then refer back to that agreement when it is tested.

quote.text: But the person who's gonna decide when that vote is is me, and I say our first order of business is putting out word that Harvey Specter is the new managing partner.
quote.speaker: Harvey Specter

plays.title: Sacrifice the One
plays.target: China, Xander Feng and the Washington establishment
plays.context: Frank Underwood has just been sworn in as President. A naval standoff with China, the crisis that helped bring down his predecessor, is still running, and China's president has not returned Walker's calls for two days. Xander Feng, a Chinese billionaire who testified against Walker, is under American protection.
plays.play: Frank skips the national security briefing, saying he knows the details, and calls Beijing at once. Within hours both sides withdraw their ships. Then he revokes Feng's asylum, which has not been formally processed, and sends him back to China, where he will likely be executed. When Secretary of State Cathy Durant objects that it damages the State Department's integrity, he asks her which matters more, integrity or peace.
plays.why_it_works: A new leader's first act sets how everyone reads him. A quick, visible win on the very crisis that sank his predecessor establishes Frank's authority, and Feng is the price China wants, now that his testimony is no longer useful to Frank.
plays.outcome: The standoff ends and Frank's presidency opens with a success. Feng is taken from his hotel despite written guarantees, which shows how little Frank's promise is worth once the person holding it stops being useful.
plays.counter: Feng trusted a written guarantee from a government whose leadership was about to change. A promise is only as good as the continued interest of the person who made it.
plays.principle: A new leader should win something visible on day one, and must know who will pay for it.
plays.in_practice: In a new role, pick a visible problem you can solve quickly to establish credibility. When a partner or client changes leadership, reconfirm every commitment with the new decision-maker.

quote.text: Sometimes you have to sacrifice the one for the many.
quote.speaker: Frank Underwood

plays.title: Ragnar Lothbrok Is Dead
plays.target: The people of Kattegat
plays.context: Jarl Borg, a rival Viking lord who feels cheated by Ragnar over a promised land deal, has captured Kattegat by force while Ragnar is raiding in England. Ragnar's family and his brother Rollo are loose in the countryside, and the townspeople owe Borg no loyalty.
plays.play: Borg addresses the town. He came only for justice, he says, since Ragnar broke a sacred promise and so forfeited his right to rule. He promises fair rule and a flourishing trading town, then states there will be no law but his. He offers anyone who reveals where Ragnar's wife, children and brother are hiding their own weight in silver and gold, and declares that from now on only criminals will speak of Ragnar Lothbrok.
plays.why_it_works: Every usurper needs a legal story, an economic promise, and a way to erase the rival. Borg supplies all three, and the bounty turns the population into informers.
plays.outcome: Ragnar's family is forced into hiding and must move carefully. Borg never wins hearts, though: Rollo's raids keep Ragnar's memory alive until Ragnar returns and drives Borg out.
plays.counter: Rollo gives the right answer: keep the old leader's name alive through visible acts of resistance, so the new order never feels permanent.
plays.principle: After a takeover, supply a legitimate story, a reason to comply, and a new reference point, or the old regime will outlive you.
plays.in_practice: After an acquisition or leadership change, people need a clear rationale, a concrete benefit and a new reference point. Borg's version is coercive; the workable version is to explain, deliver early wins, and honor the past, since banning it only makes it a rallying point.

quote.text: From now on, only criminals will talk of Ragnar Lothbrok. To all intents and purposes, Ragnar Lothbrok is dead.
quote.speaker: Jarl Borg

plays.title: Walls Against an Envious World
plays.target: The people of Kattegat
plays.context: Lagertha has just seized Kattegat, the town she once ruled with Ragnar, by killing its queen, Aslaug. She needs the town to accept her rule while Aslaug's sons are nearby and hostile.
plays.play: Lagertha addresses the town directly. She does not justify the killing of Aslaug. She says Kattegat has not been ruled properly for a long time, praises it as the richest trading center in Norway, and warns that others are bound to envy its success. She proposes ditches and palisades and asks everyone to contribute, men, women and children, the fit and the wounded, and calls for an 'Aye'. By the time Aslaug's son Ubbe visits, the works are well underway, and he admits the town is worth defending.
plays.why_it_works: A shared outside threat and a common project move the conversation from how she took power to what the town needs, and taking part in the work builds buy-in. The public 'Aye' gives her rule a form of consent it did not have when she took the hall.
plays.outcome: The town backs her and the defenses are built, which later hold off a raid (S04E19). Most accept her rule, though Aslaug's son Ivar still wants revenge.
plays.counter: Her opponents could have kept attention on Aslaug's killing, as Ivar tries to do, but without allies his demand for justice finds no audience.
plays.principle: After taking power, give people a shared threat and a shared project, so the question becomes the future and not how you got there.
plays.in_practice: A new leader taking over a team after a messy change should rally people around a concrete common goal, such as a competitive threat to address, and invite everyone to contribute to it.

quote.text: Which means, that others are bound to be envious of our success.
quote.speaker: Lagertha

plays.title: I Sent Him
plays.target: Jack Soloff (and Harvey Specter)
plays.context: After Harvey Specter retaliates against Jack Soloff for the pay-formula vote, Jack storms into the managing partner's office and demands that Jessica Pearson put her 'dog' Harvey on a leash, suggesting that if she cannot control Harvey she should not control the firm.
plays.play: Jessica tells Jack that when he went after Harvey he went after her, and that she is the one who sent Harvey after him. She reminds Jack she has just put more money in every other partner's pocket, warns him that shady tactics only work so many times, and dares him to take her on. Afterwards she tells Harvey that she claimed his attack as her own idea, and that it should have been.
plays.why_it_works: Claiming the rogue act as her policy removes the charge that she has lost control and turns Harvey's revenge into a demonstration of her power. It also recasts Jack's move against Harvey as a challenge to the managing partner, which few partners will back.
plays.outcome: Jack is put on notice, and Jessica uses the moment to push Harvey to fix his own problems.
plays.counter: Jack could have kept Jessica neutral by fighting Harvey only on issues where she had no stake.
plays.principle: When a subordinate goes rogue, own it in public and correct it in private.
plays.in_practice: If a team member takes an aggressive action that reflects on you, back it to outsiders as your call so your authority holds, then hold the team member accountable behind closed doors.

quote.text: When you went after Harvey, you went after me, which is why I'm the one that sent him after you in the first place.
quote.speaker: Jessica Pearson

plays.title: Light and Dark Succession
plays.target: Duke and Charlie Shelby (and the family)
plays.context: Tommy Shelby believes he has 12 to 18 months to live and needs to settle both his legitimate and criminal affairs. His sister-in-law Esme has brought him Duke, a son Tommy never knew he had: an illiterate fairground thief who rejects the Shelby name.
plays.play: Tommy introduces Duke to the family but says he must earn his membership. When Duke steals from the betting shop and wants to leave, Tommy tells him the unromantic truth: his mother stole Tommy's watch and invented the story of the noble father she gave him. Then he offers Duke a future: his business has two sides, light and dark, and he needs someone for each, and his son Charlie will take the light. In S06E06 a senior member of the family shows Duke the armory, tests whether he has killed and can keep a secret, and tells him he will be a general one day.
plays.why_it_works: Telling a proud young man the truth earns more respect than flattery, and matching heirs to what each is suited for avoids a fight over one crown. Testing Duke through others lets Tommy assess him without seeming to.
plays.outcome: Duke stays and plays a key part in the final purge, including the test of his cousin Finn's loyalty, and the succession is in place when Tommy leaves.
plays.counter: Finn, passed over and outranked by a newcomer, resents Duke ('You're not family!'); succession by appointment creates losers who need managing.
plays.principle: Plan succession by role: give each heir the part they are suited for, and test them before you hand over the keys.
plays.in_practice: When planning who takes over parts of your business, split responsibilities by strength and let candidates prove themselves on real work. Tell them hard truths directly, and look after the people who are passed over.

quote.text: My business has two sides. Light and dark. I'll need someone for each.
quote.speaker: Tommy Shelby

plays.title: No Bricks From the Wall
plays.strategist: Tommy Shelby (with Polly and Arthur proposing the alternative)
plays.target: Vicente Changretta and his son Angel
plays.context: The Shelbys have burned down Angel Changretta's restaurant to stop him courting their cousin Lizzie, and Angel's father Vicente, head of an Italian gang, demands respect. Tommy's brother Arthur wants to apologize, and his aunt Polly arranges a compromise in which Lizzie takes the blame so nobody loses face. Tommy's brother John ignores both and cuts Angel.
plays.play: Tommy calls a family meeting and mocks the options of 'Mr Apologise or Mrs Compromise'. While his secret arms deal with the Russians is running he needs peace at home, he argues, and the only way to guarantee it is to make the prospect of war seem hopeless: an apology once becomes an apology forever, like taking bricks out of the wall of your own house. He backs John and orders the family to take two Changretta pubs that night, keep the police away and stay off the telephones.
plays.why_it_works: Deterrence works when the other side believes resistance is pointless, and a visible concession can invite more demands. Tommy is thinking about every other rival watching to see whether the Shelbys can be pushed.
plays.outcome: It fails badly. At a charity dinner a gunman shouts 'For Angel!' and shoots Tommy's wife Grace dead. In S03E03 Tommy admits that he blames himself for pushing some people too far.
plays.counter: Tommy could have paired the show of strength with a way out for the Changrettas. Deterrence without an exit leaves a proud opponent nothing to lose.
plays.principle: Deterrence that leaves no exit turns a grievance into a vendetta.
plays.in_practice: When a partner or competitor crosses you, be firm and still let them keep face. A counterpart humiliated in a dispute will look for a way to hurt you later, often when you are busiest elsewhere.

quote.text: And the only way to guarantee peace is by making the prospect of war seem hopeless.
quote.speaker: Tommy Shelby
